of NSAIDs has been linked to as many as 30% of all hospitaliza-
tions and deaths related to peptic ulcer disease in persons aged
65 years and older.4 Although the COX-2 inhibitors are much
more expensive and no more eﬀ ective than the other NSAIDs
in reducing inﬂ ammation and pain, they have been aggressively 
marketed as being associated with a lower incidence of peptic
ulcer disease. However, use of COX-2 inhibitors signiﬁ cantly 
increases risk of stroke, heart attack, and death from coronary 
heart disease, and there is uncertainty whether celecoxib and
valdecoxib protect against GI complications.50 Despite concerns 
about physical and psychological dependence associated with
their use, opioids such as codeine can be useful for some OA 
patients with chronic pain. Side eﬀ ects associated with opioids
include nausea, vomiting, constipation, urinary retention, men-
tal confusion, drowsiness, and respiratory depression.4, 41
